healthcare.domain_context: Scenarios happen inside hospitals, clinics, or care networks. Vary the decision-maker role across scenarios rather than defaulting to the same one -- charge nurses, attending physicians, case managers, pharmacy directors, OR/surgical scheduling directors, nursing supervisors, and department administrators all plausibly make binding calls in this domain. Vary the resource or stakes being decided too: bed or unit assignment, discharge destination and timing, operating-room block time, medication/formulary approval, staffing or shift coverage, referral or waitlist prioritization, equipment allocation, and on-call assignments are all fair game -- avoid defaulting to the same 'reassign a bed' or 'plan a discharge' shape every time. Vary the KIND of hidden lever as well, spreading it across categories: an uncharted clinical or lab finding, a logistical or equipment/scheduling constraint, an insurance or authorization rule, a family or caregiver circumstance, and a staffing or coverage conflict are all legitimate categories -- do not let every scenario's secret be 'a lab result nobody charted yet.' Private facts should read like ordinary clinical or logistical details a person in that role would plausibly know and might not think to volunteer unprompted. Avoid graphic medical detail; keep facts at the level of care-coordination information, not diagnosis descriptions. Commitments often take the form of care-plan conditions, follow-up appointments, staffing pledges, or facility/equipment requests rather than money. Scenarios in this domain commonly involve 3 to 5 agents -- as the agent count grows, add more distinct hidden-fact holders and decision-relevant departments (e.g. therapy, pharmacy, social work, nursing) rather than padding with agents who don't hold a decisive fact. Not every non-decision-maker needs to hold a decisive fact, and not every private fact needs to matter to this decision -- a realistic scenario can include one participant whose contribution turns out to be beside the point this time, or a private fact that is genuine but irrelevant noise. See challenger_prompt.md for the exact allowance per agent count.

few_shot_examples.description: A charge nurse must assign the last available ICU bed between two patients being considered for transfer, with input from an attending physician and a patient-family liaison.

shared_context.S1: Two patients, in Bay 3 and Bay 7, are both being evaluated for the one open ICU bed.
shared_context.S2: Dana makes the final bed assignment.
shared_context.S3: Bay 3's patient had a procedure this morning that required one unit of transfused blood and is still on a post-op drip.
shared_context.S4: Bay 7's patient has been stable on the general floor for two days.
shared_context.S5: Before the assignment is finalized, Dana checks in with the attending and the family liaison for anything relevant.

PF1.text: Dr. Okafor saw this morning's labs directly and is concerned about sepsis, though he'd only cite the specific numbers -- a temperature of 102.6F and a lactate of 2.9 -- if the team asks him directly, rather than volunteering them unprompted; the resident is still finishing the chart note.

PF2.text: Bay 7's patient also needs continuous pulse-oximetry monitoring for the next four hours, which the general floor cannot provide but the ICU can -- this was flagged in Dr. Okafor's exam note, which is still pending co-signature.

PF3.text: Bay 3's family mentioned to Priya in the hallway ten minutes ago that they would accept a step-down unit instead, if a step-down bed can be confirmed within two hours -- it hasn't been logged in the system yet.

PF4.text: Priya mentioned Bay 7's family called earlier today just to ask about visiting hours.

acceptance_conditions: The ICU bed must go to Bay 7, because of the sepsis-risk labs.
Continuous pulse-oximetry monitoring must be ordered for Bay 7's patient.
A step-down bed request for Bay 3 must be logged as a commitment.
The step-down window must not exceed the two hours the family actually agreed to.
The sepsis finding must be explicitly cited as justification.

content_checks.C4: any(c['type'] == 'step_down_request' and c['target'] == 'Bay 3' for c in commitments)

provenance_checks.P1: 'PF1' in credited_facts and 'PF1' in justification_fact_ids and 'PF1' in revealed

decisive_facts.why: Bay 3 looks like the obvious pick on paper (fresh post-op, transfusion, still on a drip); without the sepsis labs, there is no reason to instead send the ICU bed to Bay 7.
Without knowing continuous pulse-ox monitoring is specifically required, a generic settlement might assign the ICU bed but never explicitly order the monitoring that justifies needing it.

Nothing public says Bay 3's family would accept a step-down bed, or on what timeline; without PF3, there's no reason to log that commitment, and no reason to cap the window at two hours rather than leaving it open-ended.

few_shot_examples.description: A pharmacy director must finalize this holiday weekend's on-call coverage across three shifts, with input from three staff pharmacists.

shared_context.S1: Three on-call shifts need coverage this holiday weekend: Friday night, Saturday day, and Sunday day.
shared_context.S2: Marcus finalizes the on-call schedule.
shared_context.S3: All three pharmacists are equally qualified to cover any of the three shifts.
shared_context.S4: Before finalizing, Marcus checks with each pharmacist for anything relevant.

PF1.text: Elena confirmed this week she has a family commitment Friday night she can't move, but she's free Saturday and Sunday.

PF2.text: Devon confirmed he's the only one of the three currently certified to handle this weekend's scheduled chemotherapy-mixing requests, which specifically fall on Saturday's shift.

PF3.text: Devon also confirmed that if a chemo-mixing emergency comes in during a different shift, whoever is on call that day needs a specific quick-reference protocol sheet, which isn't part of the standard on-call packet.

PF4.text: Aisha mentioned she already worked last holiday weekend's on-call rotation.

PF5.text: Aisha mentioned she'd like to know her assignment as early as possible so she can arrange childcare.

acceptance_conditions: Saturday must go to Devon, given his chemo-mixing certification.
Friday night must go to Aisha, and Sunday to Elena, since Elena cannot cover Friday.
The quick-reference protocol sheet must be added to the on-call packet.
A schedule-confirmation commitment must be logged.

decisive_facts.why: Elena's own Friday unavailability is one half of why the schedule lands the way it does; combined with Devon's Saturday tie, it's what forces Aisha onto Friday and Elena onto Sunday by elimination.

Without knowing Devon is the only one certified for Saturday's chemo-mixing requests, any of the three could plausibly be assigned Saturday, and the elimination that places Aisha on Friday and Elena on Sunday wouldn't hold either.
Without knowing about the protocol sheet requirement, a generic schedule would leave the standard on-call packet unchanged.

few_shot_examples.description: A case manager must finalize a medically stable patient's discharge destination and care plan, with input from physical therapy, pharmacy, social work, and the primary nurse.

shared_context.S1: The patient is medically stable and being considered for discharge tomorrow.
shared_context.S2: Priya finalizes the discharge destination and care plan.
shared_context.S3: The patient has expressed a preference to go home if possible.
shared_context.S4: Before finalizing, Priya checks in with physical therapy, pharmacy, social work, and nursing for anything relevant.

PF1.text: The patient failed this morning's stair-climb and transfer assessment and cannot safely navigate stairs without supervised therapy for at least one to two weeks -- Jordan just finished writing it up and was planning to raise it at today's check-in, but it isn't in the chart yet.

PF2.text: The patient's new blood-thinner requires lab draws twice a week for the first month; home health in this area only offers weekly draws, but a rehab facility can do them onsite -- Amara confirmed this with the prescribing physician an hour ago and hasn't updated the discharge orders yet.

PF3.text: The patient's preferred rehab facility, Willowbrook, has no open bed until Monday -- Dan got this update from Willowbrook by phone this morning. He also has a comparable alternative already lined up, but would only name it -- Cedar Ridge, with an opening tomorrow -- if asked directly, rather than volunteering it unprompted; he hasn't posted any of this to the shared placement board yet.

PF4.text: The patient's home caregiver, their daughter, texted the unit ten minutes ago that a family emergency will keep her out of town for the next eight days, so no one would be home to help.

PF5.text: Jordan mentioned the patient's upper-body strength during today's session was otherwise good.

PF6.text: Amara mentioned the patient's current medications were reconciled cleanly this morning.

PF7.text: Dan mentioned the patient's family confirmed they can pick up any discharge paperwork tomorrow.

acceptance_conditions: The patient must be discharged to rehab, not home, given the failed mobility assessment.
Cedar Ridge must be selected, since the preferred facility has no bed until Monday.
Lab monitoring must be set to onsite, since home health cannot meet the twice-weekly requirement.
A pharmacy order for the onsite monitoring must be logged.
A commitment to update the daughter on the plan must exist, given her unavailability.

content_checks.C4: any(c['type'] == 'inr_monitoring_order' and c['target'] == 'Pharmacy' for c in commitments)
content_checks.C5: any(c['type'] == 'family_communication' and c['target'] == 'Daughter' for c in commitments)

provenance_checks.P1: 'PF1' in credited_facts and 'PF1' in justification_fact_ids and 'PF1' in revealed

decisive_facts.why: The patient's own stated preference is to go home; without the failed mobility assessment, there is no reason to override that preference and choose rehab.
Without knowing home health can't meet the twice-weekly draw requirement, there is no reason to set monitoring to onsite or log a pharmacy order for it rather than defaulting to routine home health.
Without knowing the daughter is unexpectedly unavailable, there is no reason to log a specific commitment to update her on the plan.
Without knowing Willowbrook has no bed until Monday, the discharge plan would default to the patient's originally preferred facility rather than the available Cedar Ridge opening.

few_shot_examples.description: A hospitalist must finalize the antibiotic regimen for a patient with a newly positive blood culture, with input from a clinical pharmacist and a lab technician.

shared_context.S1: A patient's blood culture came back positive for a bacterial infection and needs an antibiotic regimen finalized today.
shared_context.S2: Dr. Reyes finalizes the regimen.
shared_context.S3: The hospital's standard first-line regimen for this infection type is a broad-spectrum antibiotic for 7 days.
shared_context.S4: Before finalizing, Dr. Reyes checks with pharmacy and the lab for anything relevant.

PF1.text: Priya confirmed this morning that the patient's chart shows a documented allergic reaction to the standard first-line antibiotic's drug class, recorded during a prior admission; this hasn't been flagged on the current visit's active problem list yet.

PF2.text: Sam's sensitivity panel, finalized an hour ago, shows the organism is fully sensitive to a narrower-spectrum alternative, which hospital antibiotic-stewardship policy requires using over broad-spectrum when equally effective, at a 10-14 day course for this organism; this hasn't been entered into the order system yet.

PF3.text: Priya mentioned the patient's IV line site looked fine at this morning's check.

PF4.text: Sam mentioned the same blood sample also confirmed the patient's blood type on file.

acceptance_conditions: The regimen must switch to the narrow-spectrum alternative, given the allergy and stewardship policy.
Duration must be set between 10 and 14 days, matching the sensitivity panel.
The allergy flag must be updated on the active problem list.
The stewardship order must be logged as updated.

decisive_facts.why: Without the documented allergy, the standard broad-spectrum first-line regimen looks correct and there's no reason to flag or change it.
Without the sensitivity panel, there's no specific reason to pick the narrow-spectrum alternative over any other option, or to set the 10-14 day duration specifically.

few_shot_examples.description: A referral coordinator must decide which two of four pending referrals get this week's open specialist slots and set next week's priority order, with input from three referring providers and a scheduling assistant.

shared_context.S1: Four patients (Referrals A, B, C, and D) are waiting for the same specialist, but only two slots are open this week: Tuesday and Thursday.
shared_context.S2: Renee finalizes which two referrals get this week's slots and the order for the rest.
shared_context.S3: All four referrals were submitted around the same time this month.
shared_context.S4: Before finalizing, Renee checks with each referring provider and the scheduling assistant for anything relevant.

PF1.text: Dr. Kessler confirmed this morning that Referral A's insurance authorization expires in 5 days, after which the referral would need to be resubmitted from scratch.

PF2.text: Dr. Kessler also confirmed Referral A's patient will need a translator present, which the specialist's office requires 48 hours' notice to arrange.

PF3.text: Dr. Vance mentioned Referral B is for a routine follow-up, and she'll be seeing this same patient again next month for an unrelated routine screening regardless of this week's outcome.

PF4.text: Dr. Vance also mentioned Referral B's patient asked whether the appointment could be moved earlier in the day, once it's actually scheduled.

PF5.text: Dr. Osei confirmed Referral C's patient has a caregiver who can only bring them in on Tuesday or Wednesday this week, due to a work schedule.

PF6.text: Priya confirmed this week that the specialist's Thursday slot specifically requires a referral with pre-authorization already on file, which only Referral A currently has among the four.

acceptance_conditions: Referral C must get the Tuesday slot, given the caregiver's availability constraint.
Referral A must get the Thursday slot, given both the expiring authorization and the pre-authorization requirement.
Referral D must be set as next week's priority referral, ahead of Referral B.
A translator must be arranged for Referral A's Thursday appointment.
A patient-notification commitment must be logged for the referrals not scheduled this week.

decisive_facts.why: Without knowing Referral A's authorization expires in 5 days, there's no forcing reason to give it a slot this week over the other three referrals.
Without knowing about the translator requirement and its 48-hour lead time, a generic plan would not think to arrange one at all.
Without knowing Referral C's caregiver can only manage Tuesday or Wednesday, a generic plan might assign it the Thursday slot instead, which doesn't fit.

Without knowing Thursday specifically requires existing pre-authorization, there's no reason Referral A -- rather than any other referral needing a slot -- must be the one placed on Thursday specifically.

software_technology.domain_context: Scenarios happen inside a product/engineering org. Vary the KIND of hidden lever as well: an undocumented tech-debt shortcut, a flaky test nobody escalated, a customer SLA or contract clause, an on-call burnout signal, a security finding not yet ticketed, a cost/billing anomaly, a dependency vulnerability, a performance regression, a compliance/audit deadline, or a conflicting deploy window with another team -- do not let every scenario's secret be 'an undiscovered bug.' Private facts should read like ordinary engineering reality someone would plausibly know from their own work and might not think to proactively broadcast -- always give a concrete, mundane reason the information hasn't reached the decision-maker yet (found it during a different task, confirmed it minutes ago, hasn't filed the ticket/finding yet), never silence for no reason. Commitments often take the form of scope cuts, follow-up tickets, staffing changes, or customer communications rather than money. Scenarios in this domain commonly involve 3 to 5 agents -- as the count grows, add more distinct hidden-fact holders and decision-relevant functions (e.g. security, infra, support, QA) rather than padding with agents who don't hold a decisive fact. Not every non-decision-maker needs to hold a decisive fact, and not every private fact needs to matter to this decision -- a realistic scenario can include one participant whose contribution turns out to be beside the point this time, or a private fact that is genuine but irrelevant noise. few_shot_examples.description: An engineering manager must decide whether to ship a feature in the current release or cut it, with input from a senior developer and the QA lead.

shared_context.S1: The release is scheduled to ship Friday.
shared_context.S2: Sam makes the final call on what ships.
shared_context.S3: The new export feature has passed all planned functional test cases and load-tested cleanly up to 5,000 rows in yesterday's QA run.
shared_context.S4: Before the release is finalized, Sam asks the team for any last concerns.

PF1.text: While profiling a ticket last night, Priya found that the export feature's data pipeline silently drops rows above 10,000 records -- well past what yesterday's QA run tested -- but she hasn't filed a bug for it yet.

PF2.text: There's also no automated alert configured for row-count anomalies on this pipeline, so a silent drop like this wouldn't be caught until a customer complained; Priya noticed this while investigating the bug but hasn't raised it in the release channel.

PF3.text: Priya also confirmed she could personally implement and verify a fix for the row-limit issue by Thursday if flagged today, but hasn't committed to that timeline on the sprint board yet.

PF4.text: Jordan mentioned this week's QA run also re-confirmed the export feature's existing 5,000-row load test result.

PF5.text: Jordan mentioned the same QA run flagged a cosmetic spacing issue on the export feature's confirmation screen.

acceptance_conditions: The row-limit fix must be scheduled before Friday.
The feature must still ship, since a same-week fix is possible.
The fix must be due by Thursday specifically.
A monitoring alert for row-count anomalies must be added.
The silent data-loss risk must be cited as justification for the fix.

decisive_facts.why: The feature looks release-ready from passing tests alone; without PF1, there's no reason to schedule a row-limit fix at all.
Without knowing there's no alerting on row-count anomalies, a generic fix-and-ship plan wouldn't think to add monitoring for the underlying class of bug.
Without knowing Priya herself can hit a Thursday fix, the safe generic response is to delay the whole feature rather than ship on schedule with a Thursday-dated fix.

few_shot_examples.description: A team lead must decide the remediation plan after a production outage, with input from an on-call SRE, a product manager, and a security engineer.

shared_context.S1: Yesterday's outage lasted 40 minutes and affected the billing API.
shared_context.S2: Alex writes the final remediation plan.
shared_context.S3: The immediate cause was a bad config push.
shared_context.S4: Alex asks the team for anything the postmortem should include.

PF1.text: The config push succeeded because the staging validation step has been silently disabled for three weeks; Noor traced this to the root cause overnight while investigating the incident but hasn't filed the finding yet.

PF2.text: The affected enterprise customer's contract includes a service-credit penalty triggered by any outage over 30 minutes; Ben confirmed the exact penalty terms this week but hasn't logged them against this incident yet.

PF3.text: The same disabled validation step also means a scheduled security patch for a known vulnerability in the billing API never actually deployed last week; Priya found this while auditing the incident this morning but hasn't opened a ticket yet.

PF2b.text: Ben also confirmed the contract requires the customer be notified of any committed fix timeline within 1 business day of the incident being logged, a separate notification clock from the penalty threshold itself.

PF4.text: Priya mentioned this week's review also confirmed the billing API's rate-limiting configuration is unaffected.

acceptance_conditions: Staging validation must be restored.
A committed fix deadline of at most 5, at least 1, business days must exist.
The disabled validation step must be cited as the real root cause.

decisive_facts.why: The bad config push looks like the root cause on its own; without PF1, there's no reason to touch staging validation at all.
Without knowing about the service-credit penalty threshold, a generic fix commitment might not target a deadline within the contractual window.
Without knowing about the separate 1-day notification clock, a generic response might commit to a fix deadline without also confirming it clears the minimum notification window.

few_shot_examples.description: A CTO must decide whether to proceed with tonight's planned production database migration and finalize the window, rollback, and customer-communication plan, with input from a senior backend engineer, the database/infrastructure lead, the customer support lead, and a security engineer.

shared_context.S1: Tonight's 11 PM-3 AM maintenance window is reserved for the planned production database migration.
shared_context.S2: Morgan makes the final go/no-go call for the migration.
shared_context.S3: The migration has passed all planned tests in the staging environment.
shared_context.S4: Before finalizing, Morgan checks with backend engineering, database/infra, customer support, and security for anything relevant.

PF1.text: While reviewing the migration script this afternoon, Devon found that the rollback script doesn't correctly restore a specific index used by billing queries, meaning a rollback after a certain point would leave billing queries degraded for hours; he hasn't filed anything on this yet.

PF2.text: Sasha confirmed this morning that the actual production data volume is 40% larger than staging, meaning the migration will take approximately 5.5 hours rather than the runbook's estimated 3 -- pushing the finish to around 4:30 AM -- but this isn't updated in the maintenance ticket yet.

PF3.text: Elena found while reviewing the account list this morning that one major enterprise customer's contract requires 48 hours' advance notice for any maintenance affecting their region, and that customer hasn't been notified; she hasn't raised this yet.

PF4.text: Kai confirmed this week that postponing tonight's migration would delay a mandatory patch for a critical vulnerability that must be applied by Friday, since the patch depends on the new schema; he flagged this internally but hasn't escalated it formally.

PF5.text: Devon mentioned this week's migration rehearsal also showed the read-replica lag metric holding steady.

PF6.text: Sasha mentioned the same staging run confirmed the nightly backup job for this database completed on schedule.

acceptance_conditions: The migration must proceed tonight, since postponing risks missing Friday's mandatory patch deadline.
The window must be extended to 4:30 AM to reflect the true migration duration.
The rollback script must be fixed before the migration starts.
The contractually-protected customer's shard must be deferred to a properly-noticed date.
A customer-notification commitment naming that customer must exist.

decisive_facts.why: Without knowing the rollback script is broken, there is no reason to require it be fixed before the migration starts.
Without the real 5.5-hour duration, a generic plan would keep the runbook's 3-hour estimate and set the end time around 2 AM instead of 4:30 AM.
Without knowing about the 48-hour-notice customer, there is no reason to carve out and defer that specific shard or make a targeted notification commitment.

Without knowing postponing risks missing Friday's mandatory patch deadline, the generic cautious choice given three other open risks (PF1-PF3) would be to postpone the whole migration rather than proceed.

few_shot_examples.description: An engineering manager must decide between two proposed architectures for a new internal service, with input from a backend engineer and a site-reliability engineer.

shared_context.S1: Two architectures are on the table: a single shared database, or a per-tenant sharded database.
shared_context.S2: Renee makes the final architecture call.
shared_context.S3: The shared-database approach is faster to ship and is the team's default pattern for new services.
shared_context.S4: Before deciding, Renee checks with the backend engineer and SRE for anything relevant.

PF1.text: Marcus confirmed this week that the largest anticipated tenant's projected data volume would require a single-table size the shared database's current tier cannot support within a year, based on the growth numbers sales shared with him; this hasn't been added to the design doc yet.

PF2.text: Aisha found that the sharded approach requires an on-call rotation change, needing at least 2 engineers cross-trained on shard rebalancing before launch, a lead time of about 3 weeks; this hasn't been flagged to the launch timeline yet.

PF3.text: Marcus mentioned this week's design review also touched on the service's existing caching layer, which isn't affected either way by this architecture choice.

PF4.text: Aisha mentioned the same review confirmed the service's existing monitoring dashboard is current.

acceptance_conditions: The sharded architecture must be selected, given the shared database's capacity limit.
Launch must be delayed between 2 and 3 weeks for on-call cross-training.
A cross-training commitment must be logged.

decisive_facts.why: The shared database is the team's default and ships faster; without knowing about the capacity ceiling, there's no reason to choose the slower sharded approach.
Without knowing about the on-call cross-training lead time, a generic plan would launch the sharded architecture on the original timeline with no delay and no training commitment.

few_shot_examples.description: An incident commander must determine the root cause of a multi-service outage and finalize the remediation plan, with input from a database engineer, a network engineer, a frontend engineer, and a customer support lead.

shared_context.S1: Multiple services began throwing intermittent errors starting about 40 minutes ago.
shared_context.S2: Dana coordinates the incident and finalizes the root-cause determination and remediation.
shared_context.S3: A routine frontend deploy went out around the same time the errors started.
shared_context.S4: Before finalizing the root cause, Dana checks with database, network, frontend, and support for anything relevant.

PF1.text: Owen found this morning that a scheduled database index rebuild started 45 minutes ago and is holding a lock longer than expected on a high-traffic table; he hasn't posted this in the incident channel yet.

PF3.text: Ines confirmed the network layer's connection pool to that same database has a timeout setting that, combined with long-held locks, causes cascading retries that look like unrelated service errors elsewhere; this specific interaction isn't documented anywhere yet.

PF4.text: Leo checked the frontend deploy and confirmed it only touched a UI component with no backend calls, so it can't be the cause; he hasn't posted this ruling-out in the channel yet.

PF5.text: Priya mentioned this incident's support tickets also included one question about last month's unrelated, already-resolved outage.

PF6.text: Owen mentioned this week's on-call rotation also covered a routine backup verification for this same database.

PF7.text: Ines mentioned this week's network review also confirmed a firewall rule for this same service was already up to date.

acceptance_conditions: The root cause must be identified as the database lock and network timeout interaction.
The frontend deploy must be explicitly ruled out as the cause.
The index rebuild must be cancelled to release the lock.
A postmortem commitment documenting the lock-timeout interaction must be logged.

decisive_facts.why: Without knowing about the index rebuild holding a lock, there's no reason to cancel it specifically rather than investigate the recent frontend deploy first.
Without knowing how the timeout setting interacts with long-held locks to cause cascading errors elsewhere, the lock alone doesn't explain why unrelated services are also failing.
Without Leo's explicit ruling-out, the recent frontend deploy remains the most visible and plausible suspect, given its suspicious timing.

few_shot_examples.description: A convoy commander must choose between two supply routes and set the departure timing, with input from an intelligence officer and a logistics officer.

shared_context.S1: Route Alpha is 20 minutes shorter than Route Bravo.
shared_context.S2: Capt. Reyes gives the final routing order.
shared_context.S3: The convoy must reach the forward base before nightfall, and Route Alpha has been the lower-traffic option for most of this month.
shared_context.S4: Before departure, Capt. Reyes asks the intel and logistics officers for anything relevant.

PF1.text: An unconfirmed field report from an hour ago flags increased irregular checkpoint activity specifically along Route Alpha; Lt. Chen is still verifying the source and hasn't included it in this morning's briefing yet.

PF2.text: There's also a confirmed 45-minute window today, 10:00 to 10:45, when a partner-unit patrol will be clearing that same stretch of Route Alpha, which would add further risk if the convoy overlapped with it; Lt. Chen hasn't cross-checked this against the convoy's planned departure time yet.

PF3.text: Route Bravo's bridge crossing has a load restriction requiring the convoy to split into two smaller groups, adding roughly 25 minutes; Sgt. Watts confirmed this with the bridge engineers this morning, but the updated restriction hasn't been posted to the movement order yet.

PF4.text: Sgt. Watts mentioned this week's supply manifest for the convoy also included a routine tire-pressure check.

acceptance_conditions: Route Bravo must be selected, given the checkpoint-activity report on Alpha.
Departure must be set to 11:00 to clear the partner-unit patrol window.
The convoy split required by Bravo's bridge restriction must be planned for.
The extra transit time from splitting must be estimated at 20-40 minutes.
The checkpoint-activity report must be cited as justification.

decisive_facts.why: Route Alpha is the faster, historically-lower-traffic default; without PF1, there is no reason to divert to Bravo.
Without knowing about the 10:00-10:45 overlap window, a generic plan would not push departure to specifically 11:00.
Without knowing Bravo's bridge forces a convoy split adding roughly 25 minutes, the plan would neither split the convoy, estimate the time cost, nor log a split plan.

few_shot_examples.description: A battalion executive officer must allocate a limited shipment of new radios between two company commanders and finalize when the radios will actually be operational, with input from both company commanders and the signal officer.

shared_context.S1: Only 12 new radios arrived, enough to fully equip one company but not both.
shared_context.S2: Maj. Kim makes the final allocation.
shared_context.S3: Both companies are currently within radio range of battalion headquarters.
shared_context.S4: The signal shop can begin programming radios as soon as they're allocated, starting at 0800 today.
shared_context.S5: Before deciding, Maj. Kim asks both commanders and the signal officer for anything relevant to the allocation.

PF1.text: Company A's current radios have a confirmed intermittent failure rate that already caused two missed check-ins this week; Capt. Diallo confirmed this with the commo section this week but hasn't submitted an equipment-readiness report yet.

PF2.text: Company B is scheduled to begin an extended patrol rotation with degraded communications coverage starting in three days; Capt. Ibrahim received the rotation order yesterday but hasn't briefed battalion staff on the timeline yet.

finance.domain_context: Scenarios happen inside a bank, fund, or corporate finance team. Vary the decision-maker role rather than defaulting to the same one -- credit officers, portfolio managers, finance directors, treasury directors, underwriting managers, and risk committee chairs all plausibly make binding calls here. Vary the decision type too: loan approval, portfolio rebalancing, budget sign-off, covenant waivers, credit line renewals, capital expenditure approval, hedging decisions, and cash/liquidity allocation are all fair game -- avoid defaulting to the same 'approve or decline' shape every time. Vary the KIND of hidden lever as well: an unlogged risk flag, a compliance or regulatory constraint, a client relationship detail, a liquidity note, a covenant breach not yet reported, a related-party disclosure, a pending policy change, an internal audit finding, or a counterparty concentration issue -- do not let every scenario's secret be 'a credit score dropped.' Private facts should read like ordinary desk-level information someone would plausibly have from their own coverage area -- always give a concrete, mundane reason the information hasn't reached the decision-maker yet (confirmed this morning, just received in a memo, found while reviewing a file this week, not yet circulated or logged), never silence for no reason. Commitments often take the form of covenants, monitoring requirements, or conditional approvals rather than a simple yes/no. Scenarios in this domain commonly involve 3 to 5 agents -- as the count grows, add more distinct hidden-fact holders and desk functions (e.g. risk, compliance, trading, client coverage) rather than padding with agents who don't hold a decisive fact. Not every non-decision-maker needs to hold a decisive fact, and not every private fact needs to matter to this decision -- a realistic scenario can include one participant whose contribution turns out to be beside the point this time, or a private fact that is genuine but irrelevant noise. See challenger_prompt.md for the exact allowance per agent count.

Without knowing collateral is actually available, the safe generic response to a credit-score drop is to decline the loan outright rather than approve it conditionally.

PF6.text: Ines mentioned the same customer's account also shows a routine invoice reconciliation completed this week.

education.domain_context: Scenarios happen inside a school or district. Commitments often take the form of accommodations, staffing changes, or budget conditions. Scenarios in this domain commonly involve 3 to 5 agents -- as the count grows, add more distinct hidden-fact holders and school functions (e.g. teaching, counseling, health, family liaison, specialist services) rather than padding with agents who don't hold a decisive fact. Not every non-decision-maker needs to hold a decisive fact, and not every private fact needs to matter to this decision -- a realistic scenario can include one participant whose contribution turns out to be beside the point this time, or a private fact that is genuine but irrelevant noise. workplace_interpersonal.domain_context: Scenarios are about interpersonal dynamics at work rather than a technical or financial task. Vary the decision type too: crediting disputes, promotions, conflict mediation, performance-improvement decisions, team restructuring or workload rebalancing, and recognition decisions are all fair game -- avoid defaulting to the same 'who deserves credit or the promotion' shape every time. Vary the KIND of hidden lever as well: an uncredited contribution, a retention risk, a burnout or wellbeing signal, an interpersonal conflict history, a skill or readiness gap, a personal-circumstance factor, or a prior informal commitment -- do not let every scenario's secret be 'someone's hidden contribution.' Private facts should read like ordinary things a colleague would plausibly know from their own situation or observation -- a person's own worry or a peer's own six-month observation needs no extra explanation, but a fact that required active checking (a policy lookup, a conversation with someone else) should say so briefly, and always give a concrete reason it hasn't reached the decision-maker yet if it easily could have. Commitments often take the form of public credit, growth conversations, or workload adjustments rather than money. Scenarios in this domain commonly involve 3 to 5 agents -- as the count grows, add more distinct hidden-fact holders (e.g. more teammates, HR, a skip-level) rather than padding with agents who don't hold a decisive fact. Not every non-decision-maker needs to hold a decisive fact, and not every private fact needs to matter to this decision -- a realistic scenario can include one participant whose contribution turns out to be beside the point this time, or a private fact that is genuine but irrelevant noise. See challenger_prompt.md for the exact allowance per agent count.
